title: Ultra-tight multisets admit integer column potentials
statement: Let $r\ge1$ and $L_r=\mathbb Z^r/\mathbb Z(1,\ldots,1)$. For a finite multiset $X$ in $L_r$, call $X$ tight if $(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)\le2$ for all occurrences $x,y$ and indices $k,l$. A zero exchange replaces $x,y$ by $x-e_k+e_l,y+e_k-e_l$ when that difference equals2; it is symmetric. Call $X$ ultra-tight if every finite zero-exchange sequence ends in a tight multiset. Then $X$ is ultra-tight iff some $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ satisfies $x_k-x_l\le s_k-s_l+1$ for every $x\in X,k,l$. This includes the empty multiset and $r=1$.
strategy:
For the empty multiset take s=0. For nonempty X the complete finite induction follows.

Work in L_r=Z^r/Z(1,…,1). A finite multiset X is tight if

(x_k−x_l)−(y_k−y_l)≤2 for every x,y∈X and every k,l.

A zero exchange replaces x,y by x−e_k+e_l and y+e_k−e_l when the displayed difference equals 2. This relation is symmetric; call X ultra-tight if every multiset obtainable by finitely many zero exchanges is tight. These notions do not depend on representatives in Z^r.

**Lemma.** X is ultra-tight iff there are integers s₁,…,s_r such that x_k−x_l≤s_k−s_l+1 for every x∈X and every k,l.

The reverse implication has a short direct proof. After replacing x by x−s, every row has maximum minus minimum at most one. A zero exchange must have x_k−x_l=1 and y_k−y_l=−1, so it merely swaps the high and low values in these two coordinates of each row. The row spread remains at most one. The property is preserved by every zero exchange and implies tightness.

Here is a full proof of the forward implication, adapted from the actual proof of Fayers Proposition 2.2 and its induction step Proposition 2.3 (author PDF pp.11–15). We induct on r. The r=1 case is trivial. Projection forgetting the last coordinate takes an ultra-tight multiset to one in L_(r−1): every zero exchange in the projection lifts using the same pair of coordinate indices and the same labeled multiset occurrences. Hence the induction hypothesis supplies potentials for the first r−1 coordinates. It remains to extend them to coordinate r, preserving all previous bounds.

Write a_kl=s_k−s_l. Suppose bounds |(x_k−x_l)−a_kl|≤1 are known whenever k,l≤r−1 or k,l≥t+1, with 1≤t≤r−1. We show how to obtain such bounds also for k,l≥t. For t=r−1, tightness says the integer differences x_(r−1)−x_r have range at most two, so choose their integer midpoint for s_(r−1)−s_r; the potentials on the first r−1 coordinates stay fixed.

For t<r−1, if the current potentials already bound x_t−x_r, nothing is needed. Otherwise, after replacing every row x and every potential s by its negative if necessary, choose x∈X with x_t−x_r≥a_tr+2. For t<u<r, the old bounds imply x_t−x_u≤a_tu+1 and x_u−x_r≤a_ur+1. Thus x_t−x_r=a_tr+2, and both inequalities are equalities for every u. Tightness implies, for every y∈X,

a_tr≤y_t−y_r≤a_tr+2.

Form a directed graph on {1,…,r}, with an edge k→l when some y∈X has y_k−y_l=a_kl−1.

If no path leads from t to r, let T be the vertices reachable from t and let R be the complement. Change potentials to s'_k=s_k+1 for k∈T and s'_k=s_k for k∈R. Then a'_tr=a_tr+1, giving the new (t,r) bound. Any other previously controlled difference with a'_kl≥a_kl retains its upper bound. If a'_kl=a_kl−1, then k∈R,l∈T. The reverse pair has no edge T→R, so its old lower bound y_l−y_k≥a_lk−1 improves to ≥a_lk; hence y_k−y_l≤a_kl=a'_kl+1. Apply this to ordered pairs and their reverses. All required bounds hold.

If a path does lead from t to r, choose a shortest path t=k₁→k₂→⋯→k_h=r and labeled occurrences y₁,…,y_(h−1) witnessing its edges. Its vertices are distinct. Write z=y−s for each witness. On the first r−1 coordinates every such z has spread at most one, by the old bounds. Therefore one occurrence cannot witness two edges both ending before r: their low-to-high values would give the shortcut k_m→k_(n+1) for m<n. Nor can it witness an earlier edge and the last edge: a last-edge witness has z_(k_(h−1))=z_r−1; tightness against the chosen x gives z_k−z_r≥−1 for every k<r, while spread at most one on the first r−1 coordinates gives z_k−z_r≤0. An earlier edge witnessed by the same row would thus start at z_r−1, giving a shortcut from its starting vertex directly to r. Hence all edge witnesses are distinct occurrences.

For each k<r, x_k−x_r≥a_kr+1: for k≥t this was proved above, and for k<t use x_k−x_t≥a_kt−1 and x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Put x^(m)=x−e_(k_(m+1))+e_r for 1≤m<h. At m=h−1 this is x itself. We first note why none of the edge witnesses can be the chosen occurrence x. If y_p=x, choose such a p (at most one, since edge witnesses are distinct). It cannot be the last witness, since its edge to r would have x_(k_(h−1))−x_r=a_(k_(h−1),r)−1, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Run the following downward exchange induction using only witnesses with index >p, all distinct from x and from each other. It yields x_(k_(p+1))−x_r=a_(k_(p+1),r)+1. Combining this with x_(k_p)−x_r≥a_(k_p,r)+1 gives x_(k_p)−x_(k_(p+1))≥a_(k_p,k_(p+1)), incompatible with y_p=x witnessing the value a_(k_p,k_(p+1))−1. Thus no witness equals x. This use of the induction is valid on the shorter tail because it needs only its current distinguished row and the tail witnesses, whose occurrences survive all earlier tail exchanges.

Here is that downward induction in full. We prove that some multiset equivalent to X contains x^(m) and the unchanged witnesses y₁,…,y_m, and that x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. The base uses the original X: tightness between x and y_(h−1) says their (k_(h−1),r) differences, which differ by at least two, differ by exactly two, forcing the claimed equality and giving a permitted zero exchange for the next stage. For the induction step, perform the zero exchange between x^(m+1) and y_(m+1) in coordinates k_(m+1),k_(m+2). It creates x^(m) and leaves all earlier witnesses unchanged because their occurrences are distinct. For m≤h−2 neither k_m nor k_(m+1) is r. The already proved equality at k_(m+1), and the lower bound at k_m, give

x^(m)_(k_m)−x^(m)_(k_(m+1)) ≥ a_(k_m,k_(m+1))+1 = (y_m,_(k_m)−y_m,_(k_(m+1)))+2.

The resulting multiset is tight by ultra-tightness. Therefore equality holds, supplying the next zero exchange and forcing x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. This completes the induction.
At m=1 the conclusion is x_t−x_r=a_tr+1, contradicting x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Therefore an ultra-tight multiset cannot fall in this second case.

This extends the bounds at each t=r−1,r−2,…,1. The r induction proves the lemma. The proof uses only finite multisets and integer arithmetic.

title: Charged core matrices admit size descent and minimum-size switch connectivity
statement: Fix finite $e\ge2$, $\ell\ge1$ and charges $c_a\in\mathbb Z$. Give nodes of component $a$ residue $c_a+j-i\pmod e$. Write $C_i$ for residue counts and $\delta_i$ for removable minus addable $i$-nodes. Then $\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i$, $m_i=\#\{a:c_a\equiv i\}$, with both neighboring terms retained at $e=2$. Equal hubs and equal size are equivalent to equal content. For componentwise $e$-cores, let $b_{ia}$ be the largest charged beta bead on runner $i$ and $t_{ia}=(b_{ia}-i)/e$. Cores of fixed hub/charges correspond exactly to integer matrices with fixed row sums and column sums $c_a-e$; for two such cores, their size difference is $\frac e2$ times the difference of $\sum t_{ia}^2$. Every nonminimum-size core admits a finite same-hub core-switch path that never increases size and ends at a smaller core. Every pair of minimum-size cores is connected by equal-size switches. A switch subtracts1 at $(i,a),(j,b)$ and adds1 at $(i,b),(j,a)$; each path switch can be oriented with $\gamma=t_{ia}-t_{ib}-t_{ja}+t_{jb}\ge2$, giving size change $-e(\gamma-2)$. Minimum cores exist for every nonempty fixed-hub class.
strategy:
**Given:** the charged beta/core conventions and [[lem-ultra-tight-multisets-admit-column-potentials]].

Fix e≥2, ℓ≥1 and integer charges c₁,…,cℓ. A component λ^(a) has beta set Bₐ={λ_i^(a)+cₐ−i:i≥1}. It contains all sufficiently negative integers and no sufficiently positive integers, and for large N it has N+cₐ elements ≥−N. Conversely every such set gives a partition: order its elements β₁>β₂>⋯ and put λ_i=β_i−cₐ+i. These integers are decreasing, eventually zero, and therefore nonnegative.

A bead move u→u−h, where u∈B and u−h∉B, unwraps a rim hook of length h with foot residue u−h+1 modulo e. This can be checked directly: if β_i=u and β_j<u−h<β_(j−1), the rows i through j−1 change by the shifted boundary between those two beta positions; the lost border strip has h boxes. Its lowest row is j−1 and its leftmost lost column there is (u−h)−cₐ+j, so its foot content is u−h+1. Reversing the move wraps the hook with foot residue its starting beta position plus one. In particular moving a bead upward one position on its runner removes an e-hook. Repeating packs every runner upwards. The result is independent of removal order because the number of beads relative to the negative reference tail on each runner is preserved. The packed component is its e-core. Every e-hook contains one node of each residue, so hook removal leaves the hub invariant and subtracts the all-one vector from the residue counts.

Let Cᵢ(λ) be node residue counts and mᵢ=#{a:cₐ≡i mod e}. Set δᵢ=number of removable i-nodes minus number of addable i-nodes. We have

δᵢ=2Cᵢ−Cᵢ₋₁−Cᵢ₊₁−mᵢ, with cyclic indices (the two neighboring terms coincide and occur twice if e=2).

One direct proof is induction while adjoining nodes: the empty multipartition has δᵢ=−mᵢ; adjoining a node of residue j changes the boundary count by +2 at j and −1 at each of j−1,j+1, counted twice when e=2. These changes follow by recording the occupied/vacant beta positions before and after the one-position bead move; all other adjacent occupancies cancel. The residue-count expression changes in exactly the same way. This also derives Fayers weight-paper Lemmas 2.3 and 3.1 without a Lie-theoretic assumption.

If two multipartitions have equal hubs, their residue-count difference d satisfies 2dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁−dᵢ₊₁=0. Thus the first differences dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁ are all equal; summing them around the cycle makes this common difference zero. Therefore d is constant. Consequently equal hub and equal size imply equal content; equal hubs imply sizes congruent modulo e.

For a component core let bᵢₐ be the largest bead on runner i, 0≤i<e, and define the integer

tᵢₐ=(bᵢₐ−i)/e.

The packed beta set on runner i is {i+ek:k≤tᵢₐ}. The column sums satisfy Σᵢtᵢₐ=cₐ−e, by counting beads ≥−eL for large L. Writing Rᵢ=Σₐtᵢₐ, the hub satisfies δᵢ=Rᵢ−Rᵢ₋₁ for 1≤i<e and δ₀=R₀−R_(e−1)−ℓ. Since ΣᵢRᵢ=Σₐcₐ−eℓ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Thus cores of a fixed hub and charges are exactly integer e×ℓ matrices with fixed row and column sums.

If κ,η are such cores, then

|η|−|κ|=(e/2)(Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(η)²−Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(κ)²).

To prove it, count beta numbers ≥−eL in each component. Their number is eL+cₐ, the same for both cores. Their sum changes by Σᵢ i Δtᵢₐ+(e/2)ΣᵢΔ(tᵢₐ²+tᵢₐ). From β_j=λ_j+cₐ−j, the change in this sum equals the change in partition size. Sum over a: equal row sums kill Σᵢ iΣₐΔtᵢₐ, and equal margins kill the linear ΣΔt term. This proves the formula. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed expression is an integer multiple of e.

Use the column-potential lemma just cited in the following finite energy argument.

Let T=(tᵢₐ) be an integer e×ℓ matrix with fixed margins. A switch in distinct rows i,j and distinct columns a,b replaces

(tᵢₐ,tᵢ_b,tⱼₐ,tⱼ_b) by (tᵢₐ−1,tᵢ_b+1,tⱼₐ+1,tⱼ_b−1).

Put γ=tᵢₐ−tᵢ_b−tⱼₐ+tⱼ_b. Its squared-norm change is 4−2γ. Hence γ=2 is a zero-energy switch and γ≥3 strictly decreases energy. Regard the e labeled rows of T as a multiset in L_ℓ. They are tight exactly when every γ≤2; switches with γ=2 are exactly zero exchanges.

If the row multiset is not ultra-tight, a finite sequence of zero switches leads to a non-tight matrix. There γ≥3 for some rows and columns, giving a strict descent. Every intermediate matrix has the same margins, and the descent lowers core size by e(γ−2), while zero switches preserve it.

If it is ultra-tight, the lemma provides a column potential sₐ such that each row of U=(tᵢₐ−sₐ) has maximum minus minimum at most one. For a fixed integer row sum, such a row minimizes the sum of squares over all integer rows: if entries differ by ≥2, transferring one from the larger to the smaller lowers the square sum by at least two; repeated transfers terminate. Its minimum is achieved exactly by rows whose entries differ by at most one. Column potentials do not affect comparisons of total squared norm between matrices with the same column sums, since

Σ(tᵢₐ−sₐ)²=Σtᵢₐ²−2ΣₐsₐΣᵢtᵢₐ+eΣₐsₐ².

Thus T is a global minimum among matrices of its margins. Conversely a global minimum cannot admit a strict descent after zero switches, so its row multiset is ultra-tight. Starting from any T, repeated zero-path/strict-descent steps reach a global minimum: all matrices represent genuine cores of nonnegative integer size, and strict descent lowers that size by at least e.

Now let T,V be two global minima of the same margins. Use the column potential s of T. Every row of U=T−s is balanced, say its entries are uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Since V−s has the same row sums and the same total energy, each of its rows also attains the row minimum and therefore has entries uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Subtract uᵢ from row i. We obtain two binary e×ℓ matrices A,B with identical row and column sums.

Here is a complete binary-switch connectivity proof (Fayers Proposition 2.4, author PDF pp.15–16). If A≠B, write D=A−B. Its nonzero entries are ±1, with all row and column sums zero. Starting at a +1, alternate a −1 in its row and a +1 in that column. A repeated location gives an alternating cycle. Choose a shortest such cycle, with distinct rows i₀,…,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,…,j_(t−1), where D_(i_k,j_k)=+1 and D_(i_k,j_(k+1))=−1, cyclically. If t=2, switch its rectangle in A to agree with B there. If t>2 inspect A_(i₀,j_(t−1)) and B_(i₀,j_(t−1)). If A there is 0, switching the rectangle with rows i₀,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,j_(t−1) gives a binary A' and strictly fewer discrepancies with B. If B there is 1, the reverse switch on B gives a binary B' with strictly fewer discrepancies with A. If neither condition holds, D there is +1 and a shorter alternating cycle exists, contradicting minimality. Induct on the discrepancy count; every binary switch preserves margins. Hence A and B are connected by binary switches.

Lifting these binary switches to T gives switches with γ=2 and thus preserves core size and hub. Therefore any two minimum-size cores of a given hub and fixed charges are connected by equal-size elementary core switches. Any nonminimum core admits a core-switch path that preserves hub, never increases size, and ends at strictly smaller size. These are exactly the finite-e descent and reduced-core connectivity facts consumed by the Lyle–Mathas max-weight argument. This proves F locally without Fayers' weight nonnegativity, pairwise-weight formula, or matrix-alignment Proposition 2.5 as additional inputs.

title: Cyclotomic Jantzen equivalence is Schur and Hecke block linkage
strategy:
**Given:** [[thm-cyclotomic-schur-standards-and-schur-functor-control-block-linkage]] supplies standard block purity, shared-factor linkage, unitriangular standard K0 basis, and the actual Schur/Specht block correspondence. [[thm-cyclotomic-schur-jantzen-sum-formula-from-rim-hook-valuations]] supplies the terminating radical-first Jantzen formula.

The classes [Δ(λ)] form a Z-basis of K₀(C), since the matrix to simple classes is triangular with diagonal one. If Jλμ≠0, project the Jantzen sum identity to all blocks other than the block of Δ(λ). Its left side is zero, because Δ(λ)^i are submodules of the block-pure module Δ(λ). Its right side is a Z-linear combination of standard classes in the other blocks. Basis independence forces their coefficients to vanish. Hence Δ(μ) is in the block of Δ(λ).

Conversely put dλμ=[Δ(λ):L(μ)]. For λ≠μ, Δ(λ)^1=rad Δ(λ) contains every factor L(μ) of Δ(λ). Since all higher filtration terms lie in this radical, the coefficient of [L(μ)] in the left side of J is nonzero iff dλμ≠0. On the right it is Σν Jλν dνμ. If this integer is nonzero, at least one ν has Jλν≠0 and dνμ≠0, with λ>ν≥μ. Repeating decreases strictly in the finite dominance poset until ν=μ. This makes λ and μ Jantzen-connected. Using Q's block-linkage property now proves that two Δ's share a block iff their indices are Jantzen-connected. This argument proves LM Proposition 2.9 rather than merely citing it.

The established Schur/Specht block correspondence in [[thm-cyclotomic-schur-standards-and-schur-functor-control-block-linkage]] now transfers this equivalence to Hecke Specht modules. In rank0 there is one empty standard and all positive filtration terms vanish. The proof never reduces J coefficients modulo the field characteristic.

title: Multipartitions with fixed component cores are cyclotomic Jantzen-connected
statement: Under the arbitrary-field finite-e nondegenerate cyclotomic hypotheses of [[lem-cyclotomic-jantzen-equivalence-is-schur-and-hecke-block-linkage]], any two $\ell$-multipartitions of a common rank $n$ with equal componentwise $e$-cores are $J$-equivalent, even if their component sizes differ. At fixed component sizes, the full-level coefficient for a change in a single component equals its level-one coefficient. The proof consumes the actual native21 same-e-core Hecke Specht-block theorem for all ranks, not its readiness receipt, and imports no Carter-partition classification.
strategy:
Fix the rank n and charges in the Statement. First suppose the component sizes agree. For a single component a of rank m, the actual level-one Hecke algebra is the finite Hecke algebra by [[prop-cyclotomic-hecke-algebras-of-level-one-are-finite-hecke-algebras]]. Its same-core Specht-block clause [[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]], together with [[lem-cyclotomic-jantzen-equivalence-is-schur-and-hecke-block-linkage]] at level one, connects any two rank-m partitions with equal core by level-one Jantzen edges. The Dipper–James to Murphy convention change is conjugate-dual; core equality is preserved because core(transpose λ)=transpose(core λ). Thus the exact existing clause applies over the original F without an algebraic-closure hypothesis. Rank m=0 has a single empty partition and needs no block theorem.

For two full multipartitions that differ only in component a, every contributing equal-remainder hook pair in J lies in a. The common residue factor Q_a t^(na) is a unit of O. Replacing it by the level-one factor Q_a t^m also multiplies each foot difference by a Laurent unit. Hence its valuation is unchanged, and the full-level J coefficient is exactly the level-one coefficient. Insert the level-one paths in a and leave the other components fixed. Changing the components one at a time connects all equal-size-component multipartitions with the same component cores.

If component weights differ, choose a component whose weight exceeds its target and one whose weight is deficient. A positive-weight component has a removable e-hook, by its core construction. Wrap an e-hook in the deficient component with the same foot residue: for any prescribed foot residue f, moving the lowest bead on runner f−1 down by e creates such a hook, since its foot residue is the starting beta position plus1. The changed components determine the removed/added hook pair uniquely. In the appropriate dominance orientation their J contribution is one signed valuation, with no cancellation. Equal foot residue means its nonzero generic difference is divisible by t−1, so the valuation is a positive integer. Nonzero generic foot differences are part of the exact J formula supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-schur-jantzen-sum-formula-from-rim-hook-valuations]]; no unit-difference or characteristic-zero restriction is inserted. Thus the transfer is a Jantzen edge. It lowers the sum of squares of discrepancies of component hook weights by at least2. Finitely many such transfers equalize component weights. The preceding fixed-size argument then completes the connection. Every moved e-hook preserves the component core, and all steps preserve total rank.

title: Cyclotomic multipartitions have equal residue content exactly when Jantzen-connected
statement: Let $F$ be any field, $q_H\in F^\times$ have finite order $e\ge2$ with $q_H\ne1$, let $\ell\ge1$ and $Q_a=q_H^{c_a}$. For all $\ell$-multipartitions $\lambda,\mu$ of rank $n\ge0$, the node-residue contents $C_i(\lambda)=\#\{(r,s,a)\in[\lambda]:c_a+s-r\equiv i\pmod e\}$ agree for every $i\in\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ iff $\lambda\sim_J\mu$ for the exact integer Jantzen coefficients of [[thm-cyclotomic-schur-jantzen-sum-formula-from-rim-hook-valuations]]. This includes arbitrary levels and all field characteristics.
strategy:
**Given:** [[thm-cyclotomic-schur-jantzen-sum-formula-from-rim-hook-valuations]] for the actual rim-hook coefficients, [[lem-charged-core-height-matrices-have-content-preserving-descent-and-minimal-switch-connectivity]] for charged core matrices/hubs, and [[lem-fixed-component-core-multipartitions-are-cyclotomic-jantzen-connected]] for fixed-core lifts.

Necessity is elementary. If J_(λµ)≠0, at least one term of its signed integer sum has nonzero valuation. Evaluating its generic foot difference at t=1 therefore gives zero, so the two foot eigenvalues coincide. Since q_H has order e, their charged foot residues agree. The hooks have equal lengths and the same remainder diagram. Along a rim strip, reading from its lowest-left node to its highest-right node increases content by one at every step, so its residue multiset consists of h consecutive residues starting at its foot. Thus the two removed hooks have identical residue counts, proving C(λ)=C(µ). Transitivity gives necessity for every Jantzen path.

For sufficiency let κ be the componentwise core of a member of the rank-n content class. Its size is at most n and is congruent to n modulo e. All such cores have the same hub. The core-matrix lemma gives a sequence of γ=2 zero-size switches followed, unless already minimum, by a γ≥3 strict descent. Every intermediate core has size≤n and the same hub, so adding (n−core-size)/e e-hooks produces a rank-n multipartition of the same content by the equal-hub/equal-size clause.

The following explicit one-hook lift supplies a Jantzen edge across every oriented core switch.

This section is a local combinatorial proof; its Jantzen interpretation uses the exact declared local formula.

Let κ' be obtained from κ by the oriented switch in rows i,j and components a,b above, with γ≥2. Then |κ'|=|κ|−eD, D=γ−2≥0. Write

u=i+etᵢₐ, v=j+e(tⱼₐ+1), v'=j+etⱼ_b, u'=i+e(tᵢ_b+1).

In component a, the core switch removes bead u and inserts v. In component b it removes bead v' and inserts u'. Let w=(n−|κ|)/e≥0. Form λ by moving the lowest bead u of κ's i-runner in component a to u+ew (adding w e-hooks on this runner). Form μ from κ' by moving its lowest bead v on the j-runner in component a to v+e(w+D). Both have size n, the same hub, and hence equal content.

Their beta sets in component a differ only by replacing u+ew with v+e(w+D); those in component b differ only by replacing v' with u'. Since

(v−u)+(u'−v')=−eD,

we have v+e(w+D)−(u+ew)=v'−u'. Thus the two components exchange a single rim hook of length |v'−u'|. This length is nonzero because i≠j modulo e. If v'−u'>0, component b unwraps and a wraps a hook with foot residue i+1 modulo e; if it is negative, a unwraps and b wraps a hook with foot residue j+1 modulo e. In both cases the hook feet have equal residues. The hook pair is uniquely determined because distinct components change, so J's signed valuation is a nonzero integer; there is no cancellation. Hence λ and μ are Jantzen-connected by one edge. This supplies the detail abbreviated in Lyle–Mathas Lemma 3.11.

The generic difference in that unique hook contribution is nonzero by the J supplier, and its specialization vanishes because the charged feet agree, so its positive integer valuation cannot disappear by reduction modulo char F. The fixed-core lemma permits replacing arbitrary lifts by these chosen lifts before and after each switch. Strict descent lowers the nonnegative core size by at least e; therefore it terminates at a minimum core. All minimum cores have equal size and, by the matrix lemma, are connected by γ=2 switches, whose rank-n lifts are connected by the same explicit hook construction. Hence every member of the content class is Jantzen-connected to every other. The empty rank has only one multipartition and is immediate. No affine-center or primitive-block theorem has entered the proof.

title: The degenerate cyclotomic Hecke center is the symmetric-polynomial image
statement: Let $F$ be any field of characteristic $e>0$, with $e\ge2$, and let $H_d^\Lambda$ be the degenerate cyclotomic Hecke algebra with the FIRST relation $f(x_1)=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z}(x_1-i)^{\lambda_i}=0$, $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i\ge1$. Then $Z(H_d^\Lambda)$ is exactly the image of $F[t_1,\ldots,t_d]^{S_d}$ under $t_r\mapsto x_r$. The proof is over the original F, for every d≥0 and level ℓ, and does not divide by ℓ or d!. The required degree filtration is proved from the independent late bounded field basis and the transported degree-decreasing cyclotomic relations.
strategy:
**Given:** the degenerate affine/cyclotomic presentation of [[def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras]], the independent late field basis [[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra-basis-and-dimension]], and the degree-decreasing DG relations in [[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-bounded-ordered-monomials-span]]. None consumes the original primitive clause(iv).

First establish the exact filtration input. Give x_i degree1 and the symmetric group degree0. The transported zero relation R_i has leading term x_i^ell and all other dot terms have total degree<ell. The bounded reduction therefore sends any monomial of dot degree≤r to bounded monomials of dot degree≤r. Independence of the retained late field basis implies that these bounded monomials of degree≤r are a basis of filtration F_r. Leading mixed relations give the symmetric-group variable permutation, and the transported relations give X_i^ell=0 in the associated graded. Thus the natural surjection from F[X_1,...,X_d]/(X_1^ell,...,X_d^ell)⋊FS_d to gr H is an isomorphism: its bounded monomials map to the degree-by-degree basis just established. This proves the PBW/gr contract P needed by the following full colored-cycle center proof, rather than assuming it from a citation. Rank0 is F with symmetric ring image F; below write n=d≥1.

Put x=xᵢ, y=xᵢ₊₁, s=sᵢ. The relations give sx=ys−1 and sy=xs+1. Induction on polynomial products gives

s g(x,y)−g(y,x)s = (g(y,x)−g(x,y))/(x−y).

The quotient is a polynomial: the numerator vanishes when x=y. The formula holds first on x and y, and the identity for gh follows by adding the two commutator formulas after inserting g(y,x)sh. Therefore every polynomial symmetric in x,y commutes with s. A globally symmetric polynomial commutes with every sᵢ and every xⱼ, hence is central. This proof uses no division by an integer or by x−y inside A.

## Local helper 2: the graded center has an explicit orbit-sum basis

For a nonempty finite subset I of size a define, in the truncated polynomial ring,

h_r(I)=Σ Xᵢ₁^b₁⋯Xᵢₐ^bₐ,

where the sum has 0≤bⱼ<ℓ and Σbⱼ=(a−1)(ℓ−1)+r. Thus h_r=0 for r≥ℓ and h_(ℓ−1)(I)=∏ᵢ∈I Xᵢ^(ℓ−1). For a cycle C with support I set C^(r)=h_r(I)C, 0≤r<ℓ. Include all fixed points as 1-cycles; (i)^(0)=1 may be inserted or removed.

For I,J with c=|I∩J|>0, direct expansion gives

h_r(I)h_s(J)=ℓ^(c−1)h_(r+s+(c−1)(ℓ−1))(I∪J).

Here is an elementary derivation. If the intersection is {k}, compare each monomial on the other variables: the forced k-exponent in the product is the required exponent for the right side, and terms with exponent ≥ℓ vanish. Next h₀(i,j)^2=ℓ Xᵢ^(ℓ−1)Xⱼ^(ℓ−1), since the only surviving exponent pairs in its expansion have equal complementary exponents. For c>1 factor each h along a chain through the c shared variables using the c=1 identity, and apply this two-variable identity to the c−1 repeated chain edges. This yields the stated formula without assuming ℓ invertible in F.

Consequently disjoint colored cycles commute. If cycles C,D meet in one letter, C^(r)D^(s)=(CD)^(r+s). If they meet in c≥2 letters, their product is

δ_(r+s,0) ℓ^(c−1)h_((c−1)(ℓ−1))(C∪D)CD.

Indeed h vanishes unless r+s=0 (and if c>2 and ℓ>1 it also vanishes). In every surviving case this is a scalar times a product of disjoint cycles all colored ℓ−1. For c=2, CD splits into two cycles and h_(ℓ−1)(C∪D)=∏ Xᵢ^(ℓ−1); for c>2 and ℓ=1 all colors are zero and any permutation is a product of disjoint cycles. These observations also show that every product of colored cycles reduces to a linear combination of disjoint colored-cycle products.

We prove that the centralizer Q of the polynomial ring in B has as basis the disjoint colored-cycle products. Since coefficients of distinct permutations in B are independent, a summand gw commutes with Xⱼ precisely when (Xⱼ−X_(w(j)))g=0 for every j. Write w as disjoint cycles. For one cycle of size a, the coefficient condition transfers one unit of exponent between adjacent cycle variables: whenever bⱼ<ℓ−1, the coefficient at (...,bⱼ,bⱼ₊₁,...) equals that at (...,bⱼ+1,bⱼ₊₁−1,...), interpreting a negative exponent as zero. Repeating these transfers moves all but one exponent to ℓ−1. Thus for a homogeneous degree k, all coefficients are equal if k=(a−1)(ℓ−1)+r, 0≤r<ℓ, and all are zero otherwise: in the latter case a transfer reaches a negative exponent before all but one exponent reaches ℓ−1. The solution space for that cycle is exactly the span of h₀,…,h_(ℓ−1). For disjoint cycles the equations involve disjoint variable sets, so successively equating coefficients in the ordinary truncated monomial basis gives the tensor product of these solution spaces. This also covers ℓ=1 directly. Hence Q has the claimed basis; independence follows from distinct permutation coefficients and distinct monomial degrees on each cycle support.

Conjugation by Sₙ permutes this basis. Invariance under a permutation action has orbit sums as basis in every characteristic: a coefficient is constant on its orbit; no averaging or division by n! is used. A colored cycle type λ consists of the lengths of the cycles of each color 0,…,ℓ−1. Its orbit sum zλ is central, and every central element of B is a unique linear combination of the zλ. The homogeneous degree is

D(λ)=Σ_cycles ((length−1)(ℓ−1)+color).

Define U(λ) as the total number of letters in the cycles except fixed points of color zero. This is the support statistic for the triangular argument below.

## Local helper 3: symmetric polynomials lift the entire graded center

Define Yᵢ(k) as follows. Write k=(a−1)ℓ+r, a≥1, 0≤r<ℓ. Set

Yᵢ(k)=Σ_(distinct j₁,…,j_(a−1)<i) (j₁⋯j_(a−1)i)^(r).

Thus Yᵢ(r)=Xᵢ^r for r<ℓ, and Yᵢ(ℓ)=Σ_(j<i)(ji)^(0). We establish the filtered symbol formula:

xᵢ^k lies in filtration degree d=(a−1)(ℓ−1)+r;
its degree-d symbol is Yᵢ(k) if r>0;
if r=0 it is Yᵢ(k) plus a linear combination of disjoint cycles all colored ℓ−1, involving i and at most a−1 letters.

For k=ℓ use the cyclotomic relation at i=1 and then induct on i with

xᵢ₊₁^ℓ=sᵢxᵢ^ℓsᵢ+Σ_(t=0)^(ℓ−1)xᵢ^t xᵢ₊₁^(ℓ−1−t)sᵢ.

The identity follows by telescoping from xᵢ₊₁=sᵢxᵢsᵢ+sᵢ. Taking degree-(ℓ−1) symbols yields Yᵢ(ℓ)−c₁Xᵢ^(ℓ−1). Terms involving c₂,… have lower filtered degree (for ℓ=1 the same formula reads xᵢ=Yᵢ(1)−c₁).

For k=(a−1)ℓ take the (a−1)st power of this symbol. In expanding Yᵢ(ℓ)^(a−1), terms selecting distinct transpositions (j₁i),…,(j_(a−1)i) give exactly Yᵢ(k), each cycle once: its orientation determines their ordered list. A first repeated letter makes two cycles colored ℓ−1 by the c=2 identity above, on at most as many letters as transpositions already chosen. Subsequent multiplication either adds a new letter by the c=1 identity, vanishes, or yields again disjoint cycles all colored ℓ−1 with the same support bound. Any term selecting −c₁Xᵢ^(ℓ−1) likewise has all cycles colored ℓ−1 and at most a−1 letters. This proves the stated error description by induction on a. For k=(a−1)ℓ+r, 0<r<ℓ, multiply by Xᵢ^r. Every error term vanishes because it already contains Xᵢ^(ℓ−1). The main term becomes Yᵢ(k). This finishes the symbol calculation, including ℓ=1, where r>0 never occurs.

Now associate to a colored cycle of length a and color r the integer k=(a−1)ℓ+r. Delete the zero integers contributed by fixed points of color zero; sort the remaining integers as a partition μ. Its nonzero parts satisfy

Σ_(μⱼ>0)(floor(μⱼ/ℓ)+1)≤n.

Conversely any partition satisfying this condition determines exactly one colored cycle type on n letters by adjoining color-zero fixed points. Set pμ=Σ_(ν distinct permutations of (μ,0,…,0)) x₁^ν₁⋯xₙ^νₙ. It is central by the symmetric-centrality argument and lies in filtered degree D(λ).

Its symbol is zλ plus central terms supported on fewer than U(λ) letters. Indeed the symbol formula expands it in colored-cycle products. The terms with disjoint cycles and no error have type λ; each such product occurs exactly once, since its cycles must be assigned to their respective largest letters, and that assignment determines ν and each ordered list in Yᵢ. Any overlap or error has strictly smaller union of nontrivial supports, and reduction by the cycle identities never increases that union. Its resulting orbit sums therefore have smaller U. Because pμ is central its symbol is central, so the coefficients on these smaller-support products are constant on conjugation orbits. All these corrections have the same homogeneous degree D(λ).

Induction on U inside each homogeneous degree now shows that the symbols of pμ span Z(B): the coefficient of zλ is 1, so no scalar inversions are needed. On the other hand gr Z(A) embeds into Z(gr A)=Z(B), since taking top degree of each commutator preserves zero. Thus gr Z(A)=Z(B). Given z∈Z(A), subtract a linear combination of the pμ having the same leading symbol, thereby reducing its filtered degree. The filtration is finite (by the established filtration it is exhausted by degree n(ℓ−1)); induction proves that z is a symmetric polynomial in x₁,…,xₙ. Therefore

Z(A)=F[x₁,…,xₙ]^(Sₙ), interpreted as the image of the symmetric polynomial ring.

This is an actual local proof of the center statement from the declared independent basis and filtration. It does not invoke the center theorem as an unproved input. The direct symbol argument also avoids Brundan Theorem 2.7's abbreviated adjacent-transposition calculation.

title: A symmetric-polynomial center makes split content idempotents primitive
statement: Let A be a finite-dimensional unital F-algebra, with commuting elements x_1,...,x_d and split joint regular-module generalized-eigenprojectors p_word∈A, pairwise orthogonal and summing to1, with (x_r−word_r)p_word nilpotent. For each finite multiset α of eigenvalues let eα be the sum over words of that multiset, and assume each eα is central. If Z(A) is the image of the symmetric polynomial ring in x_1,...,x_d, then each eα is zero or primitive central, and its nonzero terms are exactly all primitive central idempotents of A. No splitting-simple-module or algebraically closed field hypothesis is required. For d=0 the asserted symmetric-center hypothesis says Z(A)=F·1 and yields the same conclusion.
strategy:
**Given:** the finite commuting split-projector family and the stated symmetric-center equality. Write n=d; if n=0 the center is F·1 and its only idempotents are0,1, so below let n≥1. In each content summand the projector decomposition is a decomposition of its regular vector space, so an element nilpotent on every one of its finitely many projector summands is nilpotent there. Use this in the following full local-center proof.

Fix nonzero e=eα. For 1≤k≤n let σk be the kth elementary symmetric polynomial. Let ak be its value on a word of content α; this is independent of word order. On each p_word A inside eA write xᵢ=wordᵢ+Nᵢ, with commuting nilpotent Nᵢ. A polynomial in the Nᵢ with zero constant term is nilpotent: if Nᵢ^M=0 for all i, any product of more than n(M−1) positive-degree monomials vanishes. Hence

Nk=eσk(x)−ak e

is nilpotent on every word summand. There are only finitely many words, so some common exponent makes Nk zero in eA. The Nk commute; the ideal J they generate in the commutative ring eZ(A) is nilpotent by the same degree count.

Every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in σ₁,…,σₙ over F. This elementary symmetric-polynomial theorem is characteristic free: subtract the product of elementary polynomials with matching largest monomial, and iterate in lexicographic order. The assumed symmetric-center equality therefore gives eZ(A)=F e+J. Since e≠0 and J is nilpotent, F e∩J=0, and eZ(A)/J≅F. An idempotent z in this ring has image 0 or 1 in F. In the first case z∈J is both nilpotent and idempotent, hence z=0. In the second e−z is both nilpotent and idempotent, hence z=e. Thus e is primitive central.

Since the eα are central, pairwise orthogonal, and sum to 1, their nonzero terms are exactly all primitive central idempotents: for another primitive central b, the decomposition b=Σα beα has exactly one nonzero term; that term equals eα because eα is primitive. Every block therefore arises from exactly one nonzero eα. No algebraic closure, splitting-simple-module theorem, power-sum generation, division by n!, or level-one restriction is used.

title: Central content sectors are zero or primitive cyclotomic Hecke blocks
statement: Let F be any field and q_H∈F× have finite quantum characteristic e≥2. Use the standard cyclotomic type-A Hecke presentation, level ℓ=Σ_iλ_i≥0, imposed on the FIRST polynomial variable, with λ_i≥0 and I=Z/eZ. For q_H≠1 the roots are q_H^i and q_H has order e; for q_H=1, char F=e>0 and the roots are the prime-field residues i. Use only the early central CRT notation of [[def-cyclotomic-hecke-central-content-sector-notation]] and [[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-polynomial-spectra-and-central-content-sectors]]. For every content α of rank d, eα=Σ_(word contentα)e(word) is either zero or a primitive central idempotent. The nonzero eα are exactly all primitive central idempotents, so H_d^Λ=⊕_α eαH_d^Λ is precisely the block decomposition. At d=0 the unique sector is F, regardless of level; at d>0,ℓ=0 the algebra is zero. This is an arbitrary-level result over the original field in both branches.
strategy:
**Given:** the early central-content notation [[def-cyclotomic-hecke-central-content-sector-notation]] and finite split spectral/central-sector lemma [[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-polynomial-spectra-and-central-content-sectors]], with q_H of finite quantum characteristic e, arbitrary F and dominant cyclotomic multiplicities λ_i. These give central pairwise-orthogonal content idempotents summing to1 and the regular/module CRT interpretation. Their construction asserts no primitivity.

At rank0 the algebra is F, the empty-word projector is1, and this is its unique primitive central idempotent. At positive rank and level0 the defining polynomial is1, so the algebra is0 and every content sector is0; there are no nonzero blocks. Hence assume rank d≥1 and level ell≥1.

In the degenerate branch q_H=1, necessarily char F=e>0. [[lem-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-center-is-the-symmetric-polynomial-image]] gives the full symmetric-polynomial center over this F; [[lem-symmetric-polynomial-centers-have-primitive-split-content-idempotents]] now applies to the early CRT projectors and proves their content sums zero or primitive. This uses neither a field extension nor a power-sum generation assertion.

In the nondegenerate branch q_H≠1 choose a charge list c_1,...,c_ell that repeats each i exactly λ_i times, so Q_a=q_H^(c_a) and the first polynomial is unchanged. The actual arbitrary-level Murphy cellular basis and finite cellular head lemma supply all simple H_d^Lambda-modules as nonzero Specht quotients D^λ. The content-triangular JM helper [[lem-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-murphy-jm-action-is-content-triangular]] says every word on S^λ, and hence on its quotient D^λ, has the node-content C(λ). Thus a simple module in a nonzero eα sector has a label λ with C(λ)=α.

Any two simple modules in that sector have labels with equal content. The actual local finite-e theorem [[thm-cyclotomic-multipartitions-of-fixed-content-are-jantzen-connected]] connects the labels by integer Jantzen edges, and [[lem-cyclotomic-jantzen-equivalence-is-schur-and-hecke-block-linkage]] transfers this to a common Hecke block. If eα decomposed into two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents u,v, the nonzero finite algebras uH and vH would each have a simple module: select a proper right ideal of maximal dimension, which exists because the finite-dimensional possible dimensions have a maximum. The resulting simple modules cannot lie in one block, since the central u acts as identity on the first and zero on the second; all modules and extensions split by u. This contradicts the preceding one-block assertion. Therefore eα is primitive.

Finally in either branch, if b is any primitive central idempotent, write b=Σα b eα. The terms are central orthogonal idempotents, so precisely one is nonzero and b=b eα. Primitivity of the nonzero eα then gives b=eα. Thus every block arises from one and only one nonzero content sum. All sums are finite, field characteristic never reduces an integer K0 adjacency, and no original ResidueDefinition(iv), affine-block classification, or citation-only center theorem is consumed.
